has_angle_reason: This is a half-million-person city in the dry, cold central Kazakh steppe. Its name became a Soviet byword for the middle of nowhere: "Where?" — "In Karaganda!". The brief explains why people are there. Coal was found in the 1830s. Stalin then built a city to mine it, using Karlag slave labor and deported peoples (Volga Germans, Chechens, Crimean Tatars and others). Settlers dug their own dugouts and burned dung for fuel. Water had to be piped in by a 400+ km canal. Coal still sustains the city. That is a remarkable origin by decree and forced relocation, and the brief answers the question.

The brief reports the disagreements on dates and on who discovered the coal rather than hiding them.

It ran through five canals proportioned 1:3:9:27:81 [70][71] and was shared among seven clan sectors on a strict time basis [72]. The community still manages the system [74]. (2) The climate-beating architecture: storage below, family living space above covered alleys, and interconnected rooftops reserved for women as their own thoroughfare [W][62][63]. People still return in summer even though no one lives there permanently [W][55][56].
